indiaMissions/india-schwartz-tanjore/sum: Christian Friedrich Schwartz, a Halle-trained Lutheran pietist, spent 48 years in South India (1750–1798), building congregations at Tiruchirappalli and Thanjavur, becoming a trusted go-between for Indian rulers and the British, and acting as guardian to the future Raja Serfoji II. Around him grew a Tamil Protestant community with its own poets, catechists and pastors — above all the court poet Vedanayagam Sastriar — which also carried caste distinctions into church life and later clashed with missionaries who demanded their abolition.
indiaMissions/india-schwartz-tanjore/sto:
Christian Friedrich Schwartz (1726–1798) was born at Sonnenburg in the Neumark of Brandenburg, studied at Halle under the influence of the Francke foundations, and learnt Tamil there before sailing for the Danish enclave of Tranquebar, which he reached in 1750. The Danish-Halle mission was by then more than forty years old and had a Tamil Bible, a press and a small Lutheran church of mixed castes. Schwartz quickly became a fluent Tamil preacher and a skilled debater with Hindu and Muslim interlocutors, and from 1762 he based himself at Tiruchirappalli (Trichinopoly), where he also served the British garrison as chaplain. From 1767 he was formally employed by the Anglican Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge (SPCK), which funded the 'English mission' while relying on German Lutheran clergy — an early example of Anglican–Lutheran cooperation.

From 1772 Schwartz worked increasingly in Thanjavur, capital of the Maratha kingdom of Tanjore, and settled there in 1778. Within the fort he built Christ Church (completed c. 1779–80), and he founded schools at Thanjavur, Ramanathapuram and Sivaganga that taught in English and Tamil and were supported by grants from the East India Company and local rulers. His reputation for honesty made him a diplomatic intermediary: in 1779 the Madras government sent him as an envoy to Hyder Ali at Srirangapatna, and during the wars of the 1780s villagers and officials alike trusted him to organise food supplies. Raja Tulaja (Thuljaji), dying in 1787, committed his adopted ten-year-old heir Serfoji to Schwartz's guardianship. Schwartz secured Serfoji's succession, which was confirmed by the British in 1798, shortly before his own death at Thanjavur on 13 February 1798. Serfoji, who never became a Christian, commissioned a marble memorial by John Flaxman for Christ Church and wrote an English verse epitaph for his tutor.

Schwartz's networks spread the Tamil Lutheran church southwards. In 1778 he baptised at Palayamkottai a Maratha Brahmin widow known as Clorinda, who in 1785 built the first church there, the nucleus of the later Tirunelveli church. Schwartz trained Tamil catechists and promoted Sattianadan (Satyanathan), a Vellalar convert, who was ordained at Tranquebar in 1790 and led the first large accessions in Tirunelveli. Colleagues such as Johann Philipp Fabricius in Madras (Tamil Bible revision and hymnal), Christian Wilhelm Gericke at Cuddalore and Vepery, and Schwartz's adopted son Johann Caspar Kohlhoff at Thanjavur extended this work. The resulting congregations were small — a few thousand people across the region — but they were the first Protestant churches in India with a settled Indian leadership of catechists, poets, teachers and pastors.

The most remarkable product of this community was Vedanayagam Sastriar (1774–1864), born at Palayamkottai into a Vellalar family that had passed from Catholicism into the Lutheran church. Brought to Thanjavur as a boy and educated by Schwartz, he became head teacher in the mission school, a friend of Serfoji II and, in effect, an 'evangelical poet' at the Tanjore court, where he received the title Sastriar. Writing in classical Tamil genres — the kuravanji drama, the ula, the kummi and devotional song set to Karnatic ragas — he produced a large body of Christian literature, of which the Bethlehem Kuravanji (c. 1800) is the best known; much of it is still sung in Tamil churches. His work showed that Protestant faith could be expressed in fully Tamil literary and musical forms.

The Tanjore church also became the setting for a long dispute over caste. Under the Halle missionaries, Vellalar and other higher-ranked Christians sat apart from Paraiyar and other low-caste Christians, received communion separately or first, and buried their dead separately, while Christians kept caste names, dress and marriage rules. When the Tamil churches passed to the SPCK and then the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel (SPG) in the 1820s, and the Leipzig Mission took up the Lutheran remnant from the 1840s, evangelical Anglicans led by Bishop Daniel Wilson of Calcutta (whose 1833 directive ordered an end to caste distinctions in worship) treated these practices as incompatible with the gospel. Vedanayagam defended the old Tanjore customs as social rather than religious and lost his position in the mission during these disputes; many higher-caste Christians left, joined the Leipzig Lutherans, who were more tolerant of caste usage, or returned to Catholicism. Historians such as D. Dennis Hudson see the episode as a clash between an older, indigenised Tamil evangelical Christianity and a new, more assertive Anglo-evangelical missionary culture.

indiaMissions/india-schwartz-tanjore/leg: Schwartz remains one of the most admired figures of eighteenth-century Protestant missions, honoured by Hindu rulers and British officials alike, and Vedanayagam Sastriar is recognised as a major Tamil Christian poet. The Tanjore church showed that Protestant Christianity could take Tamil literary and social forms, but its accommodation of caste — and the later heavy-handed attempts to remove it — left a contested inheritance in both the Church of South India and the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church.
